Mesures pour pallier la pénurie d’eau en bouteille en Tunisie
items.description: La Chambre nationale des grandes surfaces commerciales, relevant de l’Union tunisienne de l’industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat (Utica) a annoncé le lancement d’un programme de distribution intensive et équitable d’eau embouteillée, afin de pallier les pénuries d’approvisionnement observée ces deux dernières semaines et de répondre à la hausse de la consommation. Le président de la Chambre, Hédi Baccour, a expliqué dans une déclaration à Diwan FM que cette distribution intensive a débuté progressivement pour couvrir les différents gouvernorats, notamment ceux du Sahel (Mahdia, Monastir et Sousse), qui ont connu une grave pénurie d’approvisionnement. M. Baccour a confirmé une amélioration de la situation à la suite d’une réunion avec le ministère du Commerce et les producteurs d’eau minérale ; les deux parties ont convenu de rétablir le quota de distribution habituel de 20 % à l’échelle nationale, après qu’il était tombé à environ 5 % au cours de la période précédente. Il a également indiqué que les enseignes commerciales veilleraient à répartir équitablement les quotas d’achat entre les clients afin de garantir l’accès à l’eau au plus grand nombre de citoyens, tout en se préparant à coordonner la constitution de stocks de régulation et stratégiques pour faire face à toute pénurie éventuelle lors des prochaines périodes de forte demande. I. B. L’article Mesures pour pallier la pénurie d’eau en bouteille en Tunisie est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’
items.description: A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis. With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations. View the full agenda here . 4:53pm - Founder Nutradevice calls for equitable access to nutritious food Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi held that creating awareness about nutritious food did not guarantee nutrition; rather, she maintained that it was worth examining “if the mother can access it, implement it, afford it and keeping in view the power of the woman in the household, can she give it to the children”. Dr Taqvi also clarified misconceptions around nutrition. “It is not true that healthy food is always expensive [..] as you don’t always have to focus on animal-based food”. She also noted that mothers in Pakistani households did not prioritise themselves. “Food is given to the family first. and then the mother eats whatever is left of it.” She also noted that stigma around weight gain was leading to nutritional deficiencies in women as well. 4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition. “The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said. She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage. “During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition. “250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said. 4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins 4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”. “Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said. Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem. 3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”. He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential. He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps… that will allow […] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.” Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce. He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition. He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc. 3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition. “We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled. “It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added. “Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added. Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun. 3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue. “Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting. “ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.” Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’ The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”. Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition. “Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said. 3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”. “We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said. Panelists at the Building Human Capital and Driving Economic Growth. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits. Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later. He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic. “If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said. 2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’ Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”. “The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said. 2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’ Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue. “Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.” “There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added. 2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’ The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”. “Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition. “It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added. 2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break 1:50pm - Lunch break The conference will resume at 2:30pm. 1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’ Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition. “As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”. She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition. Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty. “It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said. 1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition. She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”. “Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said. She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”. “If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said. Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important. She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions. 1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food. “It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said. He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said. Thomas Conan. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry. He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”. “This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021. “Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer. “So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said. 12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity. “We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy. “Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues. At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.” Benazir Income Support Programme Chairperson Senator Rubina Khalid delivers the keynote address. — DawnNewsTV 12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins. 12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world. “We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”. “In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India. “So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.” 12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges. “If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition. He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity. “So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention. “We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said. Dr Irshad Danish. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme. “It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership. “These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.” 11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region. “We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said. He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things. Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzed 11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun. 11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform. “It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”. “We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted. Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”. He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition. “The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said. 11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’ Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow. “Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said. 11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement. She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”. Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition. “This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added. Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries. “Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said. The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.” She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”. 11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone. “Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said. “Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said. 11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition. “Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said. He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience. “Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems. 10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins The session on global and regional realities has now begun. 10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting. “Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said. She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes. “Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said. ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’ Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”. “When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said. She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases. 10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations. “When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required. 10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food. “It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said. World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity. “Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action. 10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today. “It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said. “We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action. “Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said. 10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity “Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. “Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues. “90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said. “If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said. “That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said. 9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority. He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development. “We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said. “Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said. 9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either. “You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said. “With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said. “That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added. Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”. “We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said. “So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added. She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”. 9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’ In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted. “These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said. “And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said. 9:45am - Conference begins The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran. Attendees of the Act For Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

items.title: Guinée : le Premier ministre réorganise l’action gouvernementale autour de quatre pôles stratégiques
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Amadou Oury Bah, a officialisé ce mercredi 2 septembre 2026 une nouvelle organisation de l’action gouvernementale autour de quatre grands pôles stratégiques. Cette restructuration, présentée dans un document publié sur la page officielle de la Primature, intervient au terme de 53 sessions de concertation. L’objectif affiché est de simplifier l’action publique, renforcer la cohérence de l’action gouvernementale et favoriser une meilleure convergence des politiques publiques. Les quatre pôles retenus sont les suivants : Souveraineté et Gouvernance Ce pôle regroupe notamment les secteurs de la Justice, de la Défense, de la Sécurité, des Affaires étrangères et de la Fonction publique. Il constitue, selon le document, le socle de la stabilité institutionnelle et de l’État de droit. Économie et Transformation productive Il rassemble les départements chargés de l’Économie, des Finances, des Mines, de l’Industrie, de l’Agriculture et de la Pêche. Ce pôle est présenté comme un levier essentiel de la stabilité macroéconomique et de la transformation de l’économie nationale. Infrastructures et Développement durable Ce pôle couvre notamment les Transports, l’Énergie, l’Assainissement, l’Urbanisme et l’Environnement. Il doit contribuer à accélérer la réalisation des grands projets structurants et à promouvoir un développement plus durable. Capital humain et Solidarité Il regroupe les secteurs de l’Éducation, de la Santé, de la Culture, de la Jeunesse et de la Famille. Sa mission est principalement orientée vers l’amélioration du bien-être, de l’épanouissement et des conditions de vie des populations. À travers cette nouvelle architecture, le gouvernement entend ainsi mieux coordonner ses interventions, réduire les chevauchements entre politiques publiques et améliorer l’efficacité de l’action de l’État.

items.title: Worker jailed after smashing boss’ home, car over wage dispute
items.description: A 27-year-old worker, Lucasz Dabrowski, has been jailed for 17 months after vandalising his employer’s Grade II-listed home and car during a dispute over his wages. Dabrowski reportedly went on a destructive spree at the home of his former boss, Abrar Mohammed, using a traffic cone and claw hammer to smash windows and damage the property. Footage of the incident showed Dabrowski breaking the front bay windows before entering the house, where he continued the attack by throwing a traffic cone through another window. He later returned outside and attacked Mohammed’s Hyundai i800, smashing its rear windows and leaving broken glass scattered across the road. The incident, which occurred on May 4, resulted in about £14,000 worth of damage. Dabrowski pleaded guilty to two counts of criminal damage and one count of burglary. He also admitted assaulting a police officer by spitting at the officer following his arrest. Canterbury Crown Court heard that Dabrowski carried out the attack after money was deducted from his wages. The court was told that Dabrowski believed Mohammed, who had allowed him to stay at the property, had exploited him. The May 4 incident was reportedly not the first time Dabrowski had targeted his former employer. Police had been called to the property just three days earlier, on May 1, after reports that windows were being smashed from inside the house. Dabrowski reportedly caused about £5,000 worth of damage during that incident, with officers eventually having to negotiate with him while he stood on scaffolding outside the property. After being arrested and released on bail, he returned three days later and launched another attack, causing further damage to the house and car. The court subsequently sentenced him to 17 months in prison and imposed a two-year restraining order preventing him from contacting Mohammed. items.title: KMA announces temporary ban on new billboards
items.description: The Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly (KMA) has suspended the erection of new billboards across the Kumasi metropolis until further notice. The Assembly said the directive forms part of measures to enforce its outdoor advertising regulations and maintain a safe, orderly and properly managed urban environment. In a statement dated September 1, 2026, the KMA directed billboard owners, outdoor advertising companies, managers and individuals who rent out billboard spaces to report to the Assembly for verification. The affected operators are required to present valid permits and proof of payment of applicable fees for the 2026 financial year. The Assembly has given operators 14 days from Tuesday, September 1, to submit the required documents and regularise their operations. It warned that billboard structures whose operators fail to provide the necessary permits and evidence of payment within the stipulated period will be removed in accordance with existing regulations. “All affected operators are therefore urged to comply within the stipulated period to avoid enforcement action,” the Assembly stated. Operators are to submit their documents to the Physical Planning Department of the KMA, located at the Adum Ministries area near the Ghana Immigration Service Regional Command. The KMA said the exercise is aimed at ensuring that all billboard structures within the metropolis are properly authorised and that operators comply with the Assembly’s regulatory requirements.

items.title: Headies rejects claims of sidelining gospel artistes from major categories
items.description: The organisers of the Headies have rejected allegations that gospel artistes are being excluded from major award categories, saying faith-based musicians have historically competed for and won mainstream honours. The organisers reacted to an open letter by Nigerian gospel singer Gaise Baba, who accused the awards of relegating gospel and inspirational music to separate categories instead of allowing them to compete for major honours. Gaise Baba also alleged that although he was nominated for the Inspirational Music category introduced in 2024, the winner was neither publicly announced nor presented on stage. In a statement shared on its official Instagram page, the Headies said its records contradict claims that gospel artistes are deliberately excluded from major categories. “Every award season, the same claim resurfaces: ‘The Headies doesn’t recognise gospel artists. Inspirational music is shut out of the real categories.’ It sounds provocative. It travels fast. But the record says otherwise – and the record is verifiable,” the organisers said. The Headies cited the achievements of gospel and inspirational artistes such as Lara George, Kefee, Nikki Laoye and Timi Dakolo as evidence that faith-based musicians have competed successfully in general categories. According to the organisers, Lara George was nominated for Best Female Vocal Performance in 2008 for her song, ‘Ijoba Orun’, before winning the category in 2010 with ‘Keeper of My Dreams’. Kefee, they added, won Best Collaboration in 2010 alongside Timaya for ‘Kokoroko’, which also earned nominations for Song of the Year, Best Pop Single, Best Female Vocal Performance and Best Music Video. The organisers also noted that Timi Dakolo won Recording of the Year in 2010 for ‘Heaven Please’ and picked up three awards in 2015 for ‘Wish Me Well’. Nikki Laoye, they said, won Best Vocal Performance (Female) in 2013 for ‘Only You’. The Headies said the examples demonstrated that gospel and inspirational artistes were not confined to faith-based categories. “Gospel and inspirational artists have not merely been nominated. They have won major general categories against the strongest mainstream competition of their time,” the organisers said. Addressing the Inspirational Music category, the Headies said it was introduced at the 15th edition of the awards in 2022 to provide more visibility for gospel and inspirational artistes rather than segregate them from mainstream music. “Best Inspirational Single, introduced at the 15th Headies in 2022, was not created to put gospel music in a box. It was created to give more gospel and inspirational artists a guaranteed place on the Headies stage,” the statement read. The organisers said Kcee and Okwesili Eze Group won the category in 2022 for ‘Cultural Praise’, followed by Neon Adejo in 2023 with ‘Eze Ebube’ and Mercy Chinwo in 2025 with ‘You Do This One’. They added that artistes including Dunsin Oyekan, Limoblaze, Tope Alabi and Anendlessocean have also received nominations in the category. The Headies further explained that an artiste’s failure to make the final nominees’ list does not amount to deliberate exclusion. According to the organisers, each award category receives an average of 50 eligible entries, which are subsequently reviewed by the academy before being reduced to about six nominees. The awards body also responded to concerns over categories that are not presented during the live broadcast. It said the number of Headies categories has increased from about 22 in its earlier years to 35, making it impractical to present every award during the main ceremony. The organisers said they therefore operate a category rotation system, with Inspirational Music among the categories rotated out of the live broadcast at some editions. “Inspirational music is part of that rotation. That is not disregard. It is how a growing awards platform manages a growing number of categories,” the statement said. The 2026 edition of the Headies, themed ‘Africa to the World’, is scheduled for October 25 in Toronto, Canada. items.title: Ghana Navy, UPSA partner on research, digital innovation and capacity building
items.description: The Ghana Navy and the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen collaboration in research, executive education, capacity building and digital innovation. The agreement was signed at Faidoo Hall, Naval Headquarters, Burma Camp, on Tuesday, 1 September 2026. Ghana Navy posted on social media on Wednesday, September 2. It provides a framework for the two institutions to undertake joint initiatives in policy development, consultancy and advanced training. The partnership is expected to enhance the Navy’s operational capabilities while contributing to Ghana’s broader development objectives. Speaking at the ceremony, the Chief Staff Officer at Naval Headquarters, Commodore Ben Baba Abdul, stressed the importance of strategic partnerships in strengthening the country’s maritime capacity. Commodore Abdul, who received the UPSA delegation on behalf of the Chief of the Naval Staff, Rear Admiral Godwin Livinus Bessing, said the collaboration would extend beyond the basic provisions of the agreement. According to him, the partnership would create opportunities for the two institutions to identify areas of mutual interest, develop innovative solutions and jointly address complex challenges. The Vice-Chancellor of UPSA, Professor Emmanuel Selase Asamoah, described the agreement as an important milestone in the university’s strategy of deepening engagement with external stakeholders. He reaffirmed UPSA’s commitment to providing the institutional resources required to ensure the effective implementation and success of the partnership.

items.title: Christian Council pays courtesy call on Mahama Ayariga to strengthen collaboration
items.description: The Christian Council of Ghana has paid a courtesy call on the Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, as part of efforts to strengthen collaboration between the Christian community and government. The meeting in Accra provided an opportunity for both sides to discuss areas of mutual interest, including sanitation, education, healthcare, religious tolerance and the future of the National Cathedral. The Christian Council expressed its readiness to deepen its partnership with the Ministry in promoting national development, particularly through its Environmental Care and Cleanliness Programme. The Council said it was prepared to support efforts to improve sanitation and contribute to initiatives aimed at changing public attitudes towards waste management. Discussions also focused on the National Cathedral, with the Council indicating its willingness to mobilise resources from both Ghana and the international Christian community towards the completion of the project. The Council’s General Secretary, Rev. Dr Cyril Fayose, appealed to government to help create the necessary conditions for the project to progress. In response, Mahama Ayariga said the issues surrounding the National Cathedral required dialogue and consensus among stakeholders. items.title: Controlling roaming cows in Abuja not our responsibility – Police
items.description: The Nigeria Police Force has said it is not responsible for controlling roaming cattle in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, stating that its intervention would only become necessary when the animals are linked to an offence. The police spokesperson, CSP Ani Iniedu, made this known on Tuesday during a joint security spokespersons’ briefing while responding to concerns over the increasing presence of cows on Abuja roads and other public spaces. According to Iniedu, the responsibility for controlling animals, including cattle, lies with the relevant environmental authorities. “The responsibility for the control of animals is the Ministry or Department of the Environment. Where we come in is if the cow has committed an offence or the cow is involved in the destruction of your property or trespassing your property. “If that is the case, it is reported to the nearest police station,” he said. He added that the police would investigate any formal complaint involving offences allegedly committed by roaming cattle. “We will commence investigation immediately. That is if a complaint was made. If it is going out to look for cows, it is not one of our responsibilities,” Iniedu stated. The clarification followed growing concerns over cattle roaming freely on major roads and in other parts of Abuja, with residents raising fears about traffic disruptions, public safety and possible damage to property. Meanwhile, the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, had earlier declined to comment extensively on the issue, saying it was connected to national security. Wike said, “I have the capacity to deal with cow grazing in Abuja, but I won’t talk about it because it’s national security. Go to the NSA and the DSS DG. You know why I can’t touch it.” The post Controlling roaming cows in Abuja not our responsibility – Police appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Keeping children safe in a digital world
items.description: For children growing up in a digital world, being online is no longer optional. Tablets, smartphones, social media, games and streaming platforms have become part of everyday life. But while technology can create opportunities for learning and creativity, it can also expose children to risks that are not always obvious. A simple photo, video or conversation can reveal far more information than a child realises. The Breakdown One of the biggest concerns is oversharing . Children should understand that information such as their home address, school, phone number, passwords and family financial details should never be shared online without permission. Even a seemingly innocent post can reveal important details. A photo in a school uniform can identify a child’s school. A picture showing the inside of a home can reveal where valuable items are kept. A location tag can reveal where a child is at a particular moment. The risks also go beyond social media. Children can encounter inappropriate content through YouTube, television, gaming platforms, friends’ devices or even someone else’s phone. That is why simply saying, “My child doesn’t have a phone,” does not necessarily mean the child is protected from online content. What It Means Digital safety is therefore not only about controlling the device. It is about preparing the child. Parents need to combine parental controls with conversations about what children see and experience online. Privacy settings can help. Parents can restrict direct messages, comments, group invitations and location sharing. Features such as restricted modes, family pairing and supervised experiences can provide additional layers of protection. But technical controls cannot replace communication. Children should know that if they see something strange, inappropriate or uncomfortable online, they can come to a parent or trusted adult without fear of being immediately punished or having their device taken away. The Opportunity The digital world can still be a powerful learning environment. Children can use technology to develop literacy, numeracy, creativity, science and programming skills. Resources such as digital books, educational videos, Scratch and STEM activities can turn screen time into meaningful learning. The opportunity for parents is to move from simply restricting technology to intentionally guiding its use . Instead of asking only, “How long has my child been online?” parents can also ask, “What are they learning, creating and experiencing while they are online?” The Next Move Start by establishing simple family internet rules. Keep devices away during meals, after bedtime, during homework and family conversations. Review privacy settings on the apps children use, turn off unnecessary location sharing and make sure children understand what information must remain private. Most importantly, keep the conversation going. Ask questions such as: What new app did you discover? Who did you meet online? What was the funniest thing you watched? Did anything online make you uncomfortable? These conversations help parents understand their children’s digital lives without turning every interaction into an interrogation. The goal is not to keep children away from technology forever. It is to give them the knowledge, boundaries and judgment they need to use it safely. items.title: Lagos Assembly probes accounts of LGAs, LCDAs
items.description: By Ebunoluwa Sessou Lagos State House of Assembly has commenced consideration of the 2024 Statutory Audit Inspection Report on the accounts of the state’s 20 Local Government Areas, LGAs, and 37 Local Council Development Areas, LCDAs. The exercise, being conducted by the House Committee on Public Accounts (Local), is expected to last two weeks and focuses on scrutinising the financial activities of the councils for the year ended December 31, 2024. Officials of Alimosho, Amuwo-Odofin, Badagry, Ajeromi-Ifelodun, Ikeja, Oriade and Ifako-Ijaiye Local Government Councils appeared before the committee at the commencement of the exercise. The committee is examining the councils’ revenue generation, expenditures and management of public funds, with a view to strengthening accountability, transparency and prudent financial administration at the grassroots. Speaking at the commencement of the exercise, Chairman of the committee, Prince Nureni Akinsanya, said the scrutiny was part of its statutory responsibility to examine the Auditor-General for Local Governments’ report and ensure that public funds entrusted to the councils were properly accounted for. Akinsanya said chairmen of the LGAs and LCDAs, alongside relevant officials, would be required to respond to outstanding issues raised in the audit report and provide documentary evidence to support their submissions. He stressed that the exercise was not intended to witch-hunt any individual or council, but to enable the committee to discharge its responsibilities objectively, transparently and without bias. According to him, particular attention would be paid to whether revenues accruing to the councils during the period under review were judiciously utilised and properly accounted for, while expenditures would also undergo thorough scrutiny. He said the committee’s findings and recommendations would subsequently be presented before the House for consideration and appropriate action. Akinsanya urged council officials to cooperate fully with the committee by promptly providing requested documents, financial records and explanations throughout the exercise. Members of the committee present at the commencement included Suraju Tijani, Bonu Solomon, Ganiyu Sanni, Ogundipe Stephen and Femi Saheed. Other local governments and local council development areas are scheduled to appear before the committee as consideration of the 2024 audit reports continues. The post Lagos Assembly probes accounts of LGAs, LCDAs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ga Central residents protest over perennial flooding, demand urgent drainage works
items.description: Residents in parts of the Ga Central Municipality, including Santa Maria and Sowutuom, have demonstrated over persistent flooding and called on the Municipal Assembly to take urgent and lasting action to address the drainage challenges in their communities. The residents say years of recurring floods have resulted in significant damage to homes, vehicles and other property, while previous interventions have failed to provide a lasting solution to the problem. According to the residents, recent rains caused floodwaters to enter several homes, destroying household items and damaging vehicles. One resident who said he had lived in the area for nearly 30 years described the situation as a longstanding problem that successive governments and authorities had failed to resolve. He said the recent flooding had reached significant levels in some homes, damaging televisions, household belongings and other property residents had acquired over the years. “Most of us, our rooms were flooded, even above my height level. Your TVs, the properties that you’ve invested in for years, are almost gone,” he said. He added that several vehicles were also affected, with some residents reporting damage to their car engines. Residents demand proper storm drains The protesters are calling for the construction of larger and properly designed storm drains capable of carrying large volumes of rainwater. They say the existing drainage system is inadequate to cope with the amount of water generated during heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding of homes and roads. The residents also want the Assembly to develop a permanent solution rather than continue with temporary measures whenever flooding occurs. Some of the protesters also raised concerns about a development project in the area, alleging that the reclamation and filling of a section of land may have affected the natural flow of water and contributed to the flooding. Another resident claimed that a section which previously served as a channel for water had been filled and that construction had taken place on the reclaimed area. He said residents were concerned about the potential impact of the development on drainage in the community. The resident stressed, however, that he was not an engineer and was relying on concerns reportedly raised by engineers. He said the matter had been brought to the attention of relevant state institutions, including the Auditor-General and other investigative authorities, for possible examination. The protesters are demanding that the relevant authorities investigate the drainage situation and establish the causes of the recurring floods. They also want authorities to determine whether developments in the area have affected existing waterways and drainage channels. According to one of the residents, technical officials had previously warned that failure to address the drainage situation could result in continued flooding whenever it rains. The protesters say the issue should be treated as a development concern rather than a political matter. They stressed that after elections, their expectation is for elected representatives and the Assembly to focus on providing infrastructure and addressing challenges affecting residents. Call for urgent intervention Residents from communities including Santa Maria and Sowutuom say they have endured repeated flooding for years and are demanding immediate intervention before further rains cause more destruction. They are calling for properly engineered and adequately sized drainage infrastructure, improved water channels and a comprehensive solution to prevent floodwaters from entering homes and damaging property. The residents say they are prepared to continue pressing the authorities until a permanent solution is found to what they describe as one of the most persistent challenges facing communities in the municipality.

items.title: Dette française : le patron du Crédit Mutuel tire la sonnette d’alarme
items.description: Le dirigeant d'une des principales banques francaises a lance, le 1er septembre, un avertissement clair sur la trajectoire de la dette souveraine, jugee trop elevee et de plus en plus coûteuse a refinancer. J'ai plaisir à partager avec mes abonnés le replay de l'émission C dans l'air sur France 5, dans laquelle j'étais l'invité de Caroline Roux. https://t.co/SGbE59wbRp — Daniel Baal (@BaalDaniel) September 1, 2026 Dans un contexte electoral et budgetaire tendu, l'inquietude d'un patron de banque sur l'avenir de la dette pourrait susciter des prises de conscience chez les candidats. Un risque pour les banques et l'etat Invite sur France 5, Daniel Baal a declare : « Le niveau de la dette francaise aujourd'hui est inacceptable. Le fait qu'il faille la payer cher rend encore cette dette plus difficilement acceptable ». Selon lui, « le seuil d'alerte est atteint depuis un moment, non seulement sur les taux, mais egalement a cause du volume de la dette francaise ». La dette publique atteignait 117,5 % du PIB fin mars, tandis que le rendement de l'emprunt a 10 ans a touche un plus haut depuis 2008. 3600 milliards de dettes 💰 Le patron de Crédit Mutuel, Daniel Baal, a déclaré mardi que le niveau de la dette souveraine déjà «inacceptable» le sera encore plus avec la hausse des taux d'intérêt auxquels emprunte la France 🇫🇷 😱 Silence radio en Macronie 👎🏽 pic.twitter.com/U50rpVeaRF — Grumpy (@DonaldDucket) September 1, 2026 Le banquier a egalement evoque le risque d'une nouvelle degradation par les agences de notation : « Si la France venait a etre degradee […] ca nous pend quand meme au nez », ce qui entraînerait une nouvelle hausse des taux et pourrait, a terme, compliquer le financement de l'etat. Les banques et les assurances-vie, principaux preteurs de la France, seraient alors « menacees si la France etait en defaut ». Interroge sur l'idee d'effacer la dette, Daniel Baal a rappele qu'il fallait rester « tres raisonnable » : « Ce n'est pas possible de par les traites ». Il a souligne le role, selon lui, protecteur de la zone euro, qui aurait permis d'eviter des taux encore plus eleves apres la dissolution de 2024. Pour lui, « il faut esperer que l'election presidentielle apportera une nouvelle perspective a la France pour revenir dans un mode de fonctionnement qui soit plus sain, plus serein ». Fitch a maintenu le 28 août la note francaise a A+ avec perspective stable. Moody's et S&P se prononceront les 23 octobre et 27 novembre.

items.title: Houet : À Satiri, le PDS donne sept jours pour éliminer les eaux stagnantes
items.description: Houet : À Satiri, le PDS donne sept jours pour éliminer les eaux stagnantes Satiri, 2 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Le président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Satiri, Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a accordé, le mardi 1er septembre 2026, un délai de sept jours aux habitants dont les concessions présentent encore des eaux stagnantes, pour prendre les dispositions nécessaires afin d’y remédier. Accompagné de l’infirmier chef de poste du Centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) de Satiri et de représentants de services techniques, le PDS a effectué une tournée de contrôle dans le village de Satiri. Cette sortie intervient après une campagne de sensibilisation menée en juillet dernier auprès des populations sur les risques sanitaires liés à la présence d’eaux stagnantes dans les concessions et aux abords des habitations. Au cours de la tournée, l’équipe a constaté que plusieurs ménages avaient suivi les recommandations des autorités en aménageant des fosses pour prévenir l’accumulation des eaux. Toutefois, certains habitants n’avaient pas encore pris les mesures prescrites. Face à ces manquements, Emmanuel Ouédraogo leur a accordé un délai de sept jours pour se conformer aux recommandations. « Ceux qui ne creuseront pas les fosses dans le délai imparti seront astreints à des travaux d’intérêt collectif dans le cadre de Faso Mêbo et s’exposeront à une amende », a averti le PDS. Pour Soumana Traoré, habitant de Satiri, l’initiative mérite d’être saluée. « Ces actions sont menées dans l’intérêt et pour le bien-être de la population », a-t-il déclaré. À l’issue de la tournée, le PDS a félicité les ménages ayant déjà aménagé leurs fosses et exhorté les autres à emboîter le pas, tout en invitant la population à maintenir les concessions et leurs alentours propres et salubres. items.title: Inflation rises to 5.0% in August 2026
items.description: Ghana’s year-on-year inflation rate increased to 5.0% in August 2026, up from 4.6% recorded in July, according to the latest figures from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS). The 0.4 percentage-point increase marks the second consecutive monthly rise in inflation, signalling renewed pressure on the country’s disinflation gains. However, the August rate remains 0.5 percentage points lower than the 5.5% recorded in August 2025. The latest data point to a changing inflation landscape in Ghana, with domestic costs, housing, transport and other services emerging as major sources of price pressure, while inflation for imported items remains relatively low. Although overall food inflation eased marginally, sharp increases in the prices of selected food items, coupled with rising costs of rent, transport, electricity, education and other essential services, continued to affect household budgets. Food Inflation Eases Despite Sharp Increases in Some Items Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation declined marginally to 3.0% in August from 3.1% in July. However, the headline food inflation figure masks significant differences in the prices of individual items. Fresh tomatoes recorded the highest year-on-year price increase, rising by a striking 458.3%.Ginger followed with a 128.3% increase, while shrimp prices rose by 67.1% and mango prices increased by 57.7%. Other notable increases included: * Parking space and other services – 40.0% * Fresh coconut – 38.0% * Charcoal – 35.6% * Fresh green pepper – 30.5%** * Cabbage – 29.8% The GSS price-mover data, however, also showed significant declines in the prices of several items. Lime recorded the biggest decline at 33.7%, followed by maize at 31.3%. Cocoyam leaves, sweet apples, fried fish and pawpaw also recorded price reductions of more than 20%. The divergence highlights the uneven nature of food price movements, with some households benefiting from lower prices for certain staples while paying significantly more for items such as tomatoes, ginger and other fresh produce. Tomatoes Emerge as Biggest Contributor to Inflation Fresh tomatoes were not only the item with the highest year-on-year price increase but also the largest contributor to overall inflation in August. The price-mover data showed that fresh tomatoes accounted for about 21.4% of the total inflation contribution. Payment for rents followed with 14.7%, while ginger contributed 12.2%. Other major contributors included: . Charcoal * Cooked rice * Yam * Public and private secondary school fees * Bus and trotro fares * Electricity * Hotel accommodation The figures highlight how everyday household expenses, particularly those outside the food basket, are increasingly influencing the overall inflation rate. Non-food Inflation Remains the Biggest Driver Non-food inflation increased to 6.8% in August from 6.7% in July and accounted for 70.9% of total inflation, compared with 29.1% for food. This means that more than two-thirds of the inflationary pressures recorded in August 2026 came from non-food items. The development is particularly significant because many of the major contributors are essential household expenses, including rent, transport, electricity, education and accommodation. While food inflation has generally moderated, rising costs in these areas are continuing to put pressure on household incomes and the cost of living. Housing, Transport and Other Essential Costs Remain Under Pressure The breakdown of inflation across the major divisions of household spending showed continued pressure in several essential areas. Housing, water and energy recorded inflation of about 10.2%, while transport inflation stood at 10.5%. Education services recorded inflation of 6.6%, while clothing and footwear stood at about 8.0%. Food and beverages recorded about 4.7%, while restaurants and hotels recorded approximately 4.3%. The figures suggest that price pressures are increasingly concentrated in areas where households have limited room to reduce spending. Higher costs of housing, utilities, transport and education are therefore likely to remain a major concern for consumers even as overall inflation remains significantly lower than the levels recorded in previous years. Services Inflation Rises Further The services inflation increased to 8.6% in August from 8.5% in July, while goods inflation rose to 3.8% from 3.6%. This means services prices are increasing at more than twice the pace of goods prices. Insurance, transport, housing and education were among the areas contributing significantly to the rise in services inflation. The persistence of high services inflation could become an important challenge for policymakers because these costs are largely influenced by domestic factors, including **wages, transport expenses, utility charges, rent and other operating costs. Unlike imported goods, where exchange-rate stability can help contain price increases, services inflation may require improvements in domestic cost conditions and productivity to moderate sustainably. Inflation Remains Largely Home-grown The latest figures further show that Ghana’s inflation is increasingly being driven by domestic rather than imported factors. Inflation for locally produced items increased to 6.1% in August from 5.9% in July. Imported inflation, meanwhile, remained significantly lower at 2.2%, compared with 2.1% in July. Locally produced items and services accounted for 86.2% of total inflation, indicating that domestic cost pressures are playing the dominant role in Ghana’s current inflation dynamics. The relatively low imported inflation rate suggests that **exchange-rate stability is helping to contain price pressures associated with foreign goods. However, the rise in locally produced inflation points to the need for greater attention to the cost of domestic production and distribution, including energy, transport, logistics and other business operating expenses. Prices Decline on Monthly Basis Despite the rise in annual inflation, the month-on-month figures showed a **1.0% decline in the general price level in August compared with July 2026. The Consumer Price Index stood at 268.5 in August 2026, compared with 255.7 in August 2025, representing an increase of 12.8 index points over the one-year period. The combination of a higher year-on-year inflation rate and a decline in the monthly price level suggests that the latest inflation increase should be assessed alongside underlying movements in individual goods and services. Central Region Records Highest Inflation Rate At the regional level, the Central Region recorded the highest inflation rate at 11.1%, more than twice the national average of 5.0%. The Ashanti Region followed with 8.7%, while Greater Accra recorded an inflation rate of 5.0%, in line with the national average. At the lower end, the Bono East Region recorded the lowest inflation rate at 3.3%, followed by the Volta Region at 3.6% and the Upper East Region at 3.7%. The significant differences across the regions underline the varying price pressures and cost-of-living conditions being experienced by households across the country. Outlook Overall, the August inflation data show that Ghana’s disinflation gains are facing renewed pressure, mainly from domestic costs rather than imported price shocks. Food inflation has eased and imported inflation remains relatively low, supported by improved exchange-rate conditions. However, higher prices for services, housing, transport, rent, education and selected food items are keeping headline inflation elevated. The latest figures therefore suggest that sustaining Ghana’s progress in reducing inflation will increasingly depend on addressing home-grown cost pressures**, particularly the rising cost of providing essential services and moving goods and people across the country.

items.title: Bobo-Dioulasso: haro sur ces braqueurs à moto scooter qui traquent les noctambules !
items.description: La quiétude des Bobolais a été troublée en août dernier. Pour cause, des braqueurs à moto scooter traquent les noctambules dans la capitale économique burkinabè, ont rapporté nos confrères de Ouest Info , le lundi 31 août 2026. Des cas de braquages ont été de plus en plus constatés dans certains quartiers à Bobo-Dioulasso, selon une information de Ouest Info qui précisent que le mode opératoire de ceux qui s’adonnent à ces actes de grands banditisme est quasiment le même. «Toutes les victimes rencontrées décrivent un binôme à moto scooter, encagoulé et/ou en capuche muni de machettes qui surgit à des heures indues et tient en respect leurs cibles avant de disparaitre dans la nature avec leurs téléphones et les clés de leurs engins», précise le média qui est allé à la rencontre de quelques victimes. Les quartiers comme Belle-Ville, Lafiabougou et Bobo 2010 ont été identifiés comme les zones d’opération de prédilection des malfrats qui opèrent généralement la nuit. En binôme à moto scooter engoulés ou en capuche armés de machettes, les délinquants ciblent les personnes isolées dans des zones non ou peu éclairées. «Ils (bandits) surgissent et les (victimes) tiennent en respect avec leurs machettes avant de repartir aussitôt avec leurs téléphones. Si leurs victimes possèdent des engins, ils emportent avec eux les clés. La stratégie des bandits est, selon les victimes interrogées, d’empêcher des tentatives de course-poursuites ou aller rapidement vers les services de sécurité les plus proches», lit-on dans l’élément du média bobolais. Par Wakat Séra L’article Bobo-Dioulasso: haro sur ces braqueurs à moto scooter qui traquent les noctambules ! est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Campagne agricole humide: une bonne physionomie dans les Tannounyan
items.description: La campagne agricole humide 2026-2027 bat son plein dans la région des Tannounyan. Les cultures présentent, dans l’ensemble, une bonne physionomie. Les producteurs et les techniciens de l’agriculture nourrissent bien l’espoir d’avoir de bonnes récoltes. Vendredi 28 août 2026 ,il est environ 11 heures à Diarabakoko, un village situé à une vingtaine de km de la ville de Banfora sur l’axe Banfora-Niangoloko. La localité a été arrosée la veille par la pluie et le sol toujours trempé le témoigne. Lamissa Soulama, producteur à Diarabakoko, a son champ à quelques 7 km du centre du village. Sur sa superficie de 7 ha, il a emblavé plusieurs spéculations. Selon ses dires, 3 ha sont consacrés au maïs, deux ha au niébé, un ha à l’arachide et une petite portion de 0,28 ha est utilisé pour la production maraîchère où l’on trouve du poivron, de l’aubergine et de la tomate. On ne parle plus de semis chez ce producteur, il se consacre actuellement à l’entretien de ses cultures. Il dit être à son deuxième sarclage pour le maïs et ce jour, tous ses plants présentent une bonne mine. Le DR Minyemba Souobou : « Il n’y a pas de motif d’inquiétude quant à l’atteinte des objectifs assignés à la région ». Le maïs et l’arachide sont dans la phase de croissance végétative et certaines cultures maraichères ont commencé à donner des fruits. Le champ de Lamissa Soulama se présente bien aujourd’hui. Il confie dans la foulée que son champ est régulièrement visité par un technicien de l’agriculture qui suit ses cultures et lui prodigue des conseils à chaque passage. Il a également reçu un appui des services de l’agriculture en début de campagne. De cet appui, il a cité la fumure organique et l’engrais foliaire reçus gracieusement, il affirme avoir obtenu de l’engrais et des semences subventionnés et bénéficié d’une formation sur la fabrication du compost. Ce qu’il apprécie à sa juste valeur. Il dit attendre un rende-ment de 3 à 4 tonnes à l’hectare pour le maïs, bien-sûr avec la complicité de dame pluie. S’adapterà la pluviométrie Un peu plus loin, nous sommes dans le champ de Dangouma Hema, un autre producteur de Diarabakoko. Sur sa superficie de 10 ha, il produit du riz sur 5 ha, du maïs sur 3 ha et de l’arachide sur les deux ha restants. Il a semé, il y a deux mois de cela et sa rizière, bien désherbée, présente une bonne physionomie. Il s’apprête dans les jours à venir à un premier épandage d’engrais. M. Héma a également bénéficié de labour et de semence subventionnées des services de l’agri-culture. Ce riziculteur salue au passage la décision de l’Etat burkinabè de promouvoir la consommation du riz national. Selon la responsable de l’Unité d’appui technique en agri-culture (UATA) de Diarabakoko, Djénéba Seré, les cultures de sa zone présentent une bonne physionomie avec un stade beau-coup avancé pour les céréales aussi bien que les légumineuses. Les spécula-tions dominantes dans la zone sont les céréales (maïs, mil, sorgho, riz), et les légumineuses (ara-chide, voandzou, niébé, soja, sésame). A l’échelle régionale, le Directeur régional (DR) de l’agriculture, de l’eau, des ressources animales et Le producteur, Lamissa Soulama, a apprécié les appuis des services de l’agriculture. " data-large-file="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41.png" class="size-medium wp-image-168671" src="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-249x300.png" alt="" width="249" height="300" srcset="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-249x300.png 249w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-768x926.png 768w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-348x420.png 348w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-150x181.png 150w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-300x362.png 300w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41-696x839.png 696w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Capture-decran-2026-09-02-a-11.35.41.png 786w" sizes="(max-width: 249px) 100vw, 249px" /> Le producteur, Lamissa Soulama, a apprécié les appuis des services de l’agriculture. halieutiques, Minyemba Souobou, fait remarquer que la pluviométrie en date est satisfaisante. Pour la physionomie globale de la campagne, il y a des motifs de satisfaction aux yeux du DR Souobou. « La physio-nomie est bonne même si les stades de croissance des cultures sont un peu dispa-rates », rassure Minyemba Souobou. Et de préciser que pour la plupart des cultures, les semis sont terminés depuis le mois de juillet. Les acteurs régio-naux de l’agriculture, foi de Minyemba Souobou, se sont adaptés en fonction des prévisions de la météo. « Cette année, nous avons beaucoup privilégié les variétés à cycle court et intermédiaire. Chaque producteur a pu, en fonction de sa période de semis, choisir la variété adaptée », affirme Minyemba Souobou. Une particularité cette année de l’appui de l’Etat, le directeur régional laisse entendre qu’un grand nombre de ménages des populations des villages réinstallés ont bénéficié d’une opération spécifique à savoir la dotation gratuite en motoculteurs, en semences et en engrais.
